items.stem:
A compound which is prepared from gypsum has the property of hardening when water is mixed in right quantity with it:
(i) Write common name and the chemical name of this compound.
(ii) Give chemical equation for its preparation.
(iii) List its two uses.
items.answer:
(i) Common name – Plaster of Paris; Chemical name – Calcium sulphate hemihydrate (CaSO₄·½H₂O).
(ii) CaSO₄·2H₂O —373 K→ CaSO₄·½H₂O + 1½H₂O
(iii) (1) It is used for immobilising the affected fractured part of bone, leading to quick recovery. (2) It is used for making decorative pieces such as toys, statues, etc.
items.ocr: Preparation equation came through MinerU as 'CaSO $^4$ 2H $2$ O 373 K CaSO4 12 H O + 1 12 H O' with no arrow; restored to CaSO₄·2H₂O —373 K→ CaSO₄·½H₂O + 1½H₂O (the '12' fragments are the ½ of the hemihydrate).

items.stem:
Give reasons for the following:
(a) Only one half of water molecule is shown in the formula of Plaster of Paris.
(b) Sodium hydrogen carbonate is used as an antacid.
(c) On strong heating, blue coloured copper sulphate crystals turn white.
items.answer:
(a) Only one half of a water molecule is shown in the formula of Plaster of Paris because two formula units of CaSO₄ share one molecule of water, i.e. CaSO₄·½H₂O.
(b) Sodium hydrogen carbonate is alkaline in nature, so it neutralises the excess acid in the stomach and provides relief; hence it is used as an antacid.
(c) On strong heating, blue copper sulphate crystals lose their water of crystallisation and change to anhydrous copper sulphate, which is white:
CuSO₄·5H₂O(s) —Heat→ CuSO₄(s) + 5H₂O(l)
Pentahydrate copper sulphate (blue) → Anhydrous copper sulphate (white)
items.ocr: Stem printed as 'Sodium hydrogen carbonates is used'; corrected to singular. Solution equation printed as CuSO₄·H₂O → CuSO₄ + 5H₂O, which is unbalanced — the same solution names it 'pentahydrate copper sulphate', so the reactant is restored to CuSO₄·5H₂O. Part (c) of the solution lost its '(c)' label; restored from position.

items.stem: List the important products of the Chlor-alkali process. Write one important use of each.
items.answer:
When electricity is passed through brine (an aqueous solution of sodium chloride), it decomposes. This process is called the Chlor-alkali process, from 'chlor' for chlorine and 'alkali' for sodium hydroxide. Chlorine gas is formed at the anode, hydrogen gas at the cathode, and sodium hydroxide solution is formed near the cathode.
Uses of the products formed:
(i) NaOH (sodium hydroxide) — used for (a) de-greasing metals, (b) manufacture of soaps, paper, a large number of chemicals and artificial fibres. (Any one)
(ii) Chlorine — used in (a) water treatment and swimming pools, (b) preparation of bleaching powder, PVC, disinfectants, CFCs, pesticides, etc. (Any one)
(iii) Hydrogen — used (a) in the manufacture of ammonia for fertilizers, (b) as rocket fuel. (Any one)
items.ocr: Printed solution reads 'Chlorine gas is formed at the cathode, hydrogen gas at the cathode' — the source contradicts itself; chlorine is liberated at the anode, so the first 'cathode' is corrected to 'anode'.

items.stem: How is washing soda prepared from sodium carbonate? Give its chemical equation. State the type of this salt. Name the type of hardness of water which can be removed by it.
items.answer:
Preparation of washing soda from sodium carbonate: anhydrous sodium carbonate is dissolved in water and recrystallised, so that it takes up ten molecules of water of crystallisation to form washing soda, Na₂CO₃·10H₂O.
Na₂CO₃ + 10H₂O → Na₂CO₃·10H₂O
(Sodium carbonate) (Washing soda)
It is a basic salt. Permanent hardness of water can be removed by washing soda.

items.stem: How will you show that acids conduct electricity?
items.answer: Take dilute sulphuric acid in a beaker and fit two graphite/iron rods in it, connected through a bulb and a switch to a battery, as shown in the figure. When the switch is put 'on', the bulb glows. This shows that the acid solution conducts electricity, because acids furnish H⁺ ions in aqueous solution which carry the current.

items.stem: A gas is produced when conc. H₂SO₄ is added to solid sodium chloride taken in a test tube. The gas coming out through the delivery tube is passed over a dry blue litmus paper and then over a moist blue litmus paper. Record your observations and explain the reason with the help of a chemical equation.
items.answer:
HCl gas is produced.
2NaCl + H₂SO₄ → Na₂SO₄ + 2HCl
When the gas is passed over dry blue litmus paper there is no change in colour, because in the absence of water the gas cannot show acidic properties — H⁺ ions are not present. When the gas is passed over moist blue litmus paper, the colour changes to red, because HCl dissolves in the moisture and produces H⁺ ions, showing acidic properties.

items.stem:
(i) What do you understand by the term pH of a solution?
(ii) What is the pH of distilled water and common salt solution?
items.answer:
(i) The pH of a solution tells us about the concentration of H⁺ ions in the solution; it is a scale for measuring hydrogen ion concentration.
(ii) pH of distilled water = 7; pH of common salt solution = 7, as common salt (NaCl) is neutral.

items.stem:
In the schematic diagram given below for the preparation of hydrogen gas, what would happen if the following changes are made?
(a) In place of zinc granules, the same amount of zinc dust is taken in the test tube.
(b) Instead of dilute sulphuric acid, dilute hydrochloric acid is taken.
(c) Sodium hydroxide is taken in place of dilute sulphuric acid and the tube is heated.
items.answer:
(a) Hydrogen gas will evolve with greater speed, because zinc dust has a much larger surface area than granules.
(b) Almost the same amount of gas is evolved.
(c) With sodium hydroxide, hydrogen gas will be evolved only on heating:
Zn + 2NaOH → Na₂ZnO₂ + H₂

items.stem: Why does the medium become acidic in the mouth? What is the ill effect of the acidic medium? How can this be prevented?
items.answer:
(i) Bacteria present in the mouth produce acids by degradation of food particles left in the mouth.
(ii) Below pH 5.5 the tooth enamel gets corroded and tooth decay occurs.
(iii) It can be prevented by cleaning the teeth with a toothpaste, which is basic in nature and neutralises the excess acid.

items.stem: The pH of the mouth of a person is lower than 5.5. What changes will occur in his mouth? How can these changes be controlled? Write any two measures.
items.answer:
(a) When the pH of the mouth of a person is lower than 5.5, tooth decay starts.
(b) The tooth enamel, which is made up of calcium phosphate, is corroded.
Measures: (i) Clean the mouth after eating food. (ii) Use a toothpaste, which is generally basic in nature and neutralises the excess acid.

items.stem:
Account for the following:
(a) Antacid tablets are used by a person suffering from stomach pain.
(b) Toothpaste is used for cleaning teeth.
items.answer:
(a) Antacids are mild bases. An antacid reacts with the hydrochloric acid formed in the stomach and neutralises its effect, giving relief from the pain.
(b) Bacteria present in the mouth produce acids by degradation of sugar and food particles remaining in the mouth after eating. The best way to prevent this is to clean the mouth using a toothpaste. Toothpastes, which are generally basic, neutralise the excess acid and prevent tooth decay.

items.stem: Illustrate any three chemical properties of acids with examples.
items.answer:
(i) Acids react with metals to produce salt and hydrogen gas:
Zn(s) + 2HCl(aq) → ZnCl₂(aq) + H₂(g)
(ii) Acids react with metal carbonates and metal hydrogen carbonates to give salt, water and CO₂ gas:
Na₂CO₃(s) + 2HCl(aq) → 2NaCl(aq) + H₂O(l) + CO₂(g)
NaHCO₃(s) + HCl(aq) → NaCl(aq) + H₂O(l) + CO₂(g)
(iii) Acids react with bases to produce salt and water; this is called a neutralisation reaction:
HCl(aq) + NaOH(aq) → NaCl(aq) + H₂O(l)

items.stem:
(a) Given below are the pH values of four different liquids: 7.0, 14.0, 4.0, 2.0. Which of these could be that of (i) lemon juice, (ii) distilled water, (iii) sodium hydroxide solution and (iv) tomato juice?
(b) When blue litmus solution is added to soda water, what change will be observed and why?
items.answer:
(a) (i) Lemon juice – 2.0, (ii) Distilled water – 7.0, (iii) Sodium hydroxide solution – 14.0, (iv) Tomato juice – 4.0.
(b) Blue litmus solution will turn red, because soda water contains dissolved CO₂, which forms carbonic acid and makes the solution acidic.

items.stem: You are provided with three test tubes A, B and C which contain distilled water, acidic solution and basic solution respectively. If you are given blue litmus paper only, how will you identify the contents of each test tube?
items.answer: Dip blue litmus paper into each of the three test tubes. In test tube B it will turn red, but no change occurs in A and C; this means test tube B contains the acidic solution. Now dip this reddened litmus paper into A and C one by one. It will turn blue in C, showing that C contains the basic solution, while no change occurs in A. Hence test tube A contains distilled water.

items.stem:
How will the following substances dissociate to produce ions in their solutions?
(i) Hydrochloric acid (ii) Nitric acid (iii) Sulphuric acid (iv) Sodium hydroxide (v) Potassium hydroxide (vi) Magnesium hydroxide
items.answer:
(i) Hydrochloric acid: HCl(aq) ⇌ H⁺ + Cl⁻
(ii) Nitric acid: HNO₃(aq) ⇌ H⁺ + NO₃⁻
(iii) Sulphuric acid: H₂SO₄(aq) ⇌ 2H⁺ + SO₄²⁻
(iv) Sodium hydroxide: NaOH(aq) ⇌ Na⁺ + OH⁻
(v) Potassium hydroxide: KOH(aq) ⇌ K⁺ + OH⁻
(vi) Magnesium hydroxide: Mg(OH)₂(aq) ⇌ Mg²⁺ + 2OH⁻
items.ocr: Dissociation arrows were rendered as overline/quote artefacts ('H C l (aq) \overline{{\xi s}}'); restored as ⇌. The sulphuric acid line printed 'H⁺ + SO₄²⁻' without the coefficient 2 on H⁺; balanced.

items.stem: A salt X when dissolved in distilled water gives a clear solution which turns red litmus blue. Explain this phenomenon.
items.answer:
Basic solutions turn red litmus blue, and the salt of a weak acid and a strong base gives a basic solution. So salt X is the salt of a weak acid and a strong base. For example, when sodium carbonate is dissolved in water it is hydrolysed to some extent and forms sodium hydroxide and carbonic acid:
Na₂CO₃(s) + 2H₂O(l) —Hydrolysis→ 2NaOH(aq) + H₂CO₃(aq)
Being a strong base, sodium hydroxide is fully ionised and gives a large amount of hydroxide ions (OH⁻). Carbonic acid is a weak acid which is only slightly ionised and hence gives a small amount of hydrogen ions (H⁺). The H⁺ ions neutralise only a small part of the OH⁻ ions, and the remaining OH⁻ ions stay in solution. Hence the Na₂CO₃ solution is basic and turns red litmus blue.
items.ocr: Answer printed 'gives a smell amount of hydrogen ions' — read as 'small'. The carbonic acid product was split off the equation as a stray '+H CO aq)' line; rejoined as H₂CO₃(aq).

items.stem: Describe an activity to show that the reaction between bases and metals is different from the reaction between acids and metals.
items.answer:
Object: To show the reaction between bases and metals.
Method: Put a few pieces of granulated zinc metal in sodium hydroxide solution. Warm the test tube and collect the gas formed.
Observation: On warming, zinc dissolves in sodium hydroxide and hydrogen gas is formed:
Zn(s) + 2NaOH(aq) → Na₂ZnO₂(aq) + H₂↑
(Sodium zincate)
Result: With zinc metal a strong base forms hydrogen gas together with the zincate ion ZnO₂²⁻, whereas an acid reacting with a metal gives a salt of that acid and hydrogen gas. Only a few metals react with bases, while most metals react with dilute acids.

items.stem:
Explain why:
(i) Common salt becomes sticky during the rainy season.
(ii) Blue vitriol changes to white upon heating.
(iii) Anhydrous calcium chloride is used in a desiccator.
items.answer:
(i) Common salt contains the impurity of magnesium chloride (MgCl₂), which is deliquescent in nature. When exposed to the atmosphere it absorbs moisture and becomes moist, so common salt becomes sticky during the rainy season.
(ii) Blue vitriol (CuSO₄·5H₂O), upon heating, loses its water of crystallisation and changes to anhydrous copper sulphate (CuSO₄), which is white in colour.
(iii) Anhydrous calcium chloride (CaCl₂) is highly hygroscopic in nature. In a desiccator it readily absorbs moisture and is therefore used as a drying agent.

items.stem:
State reasons for the following:
(a) A tarnished copper vessel begins to shine again when rubbed with lemon.
(b) All alkalies are bases but all bases are not alkalis.
(c) Use of a mild base like baking soda on the honey bee stung area gives relief.
items.answer:
(a) In the presence of air and moisture, copper gets tarnished and forms copper oxide, which is basic in nature. On rubbing with lemon, which contains citric acid, a neutralisation reaction takes place and the tarnished copper vessel begins to shine again.
(b) Bases which are soluble in water are called alkalis. So all alkalis are bases, but all bases are not alkalis (for example, copper hydroxide is a base but not an alkali, as it is insoluble in water).
(c) A honey bee sting injects methanoic acid (HCOOH). Applying a mild base like baking soda (NaHCO₃) on the area neutralises the acid and gives relief.

items.stem: Examine the figure given below and describe the experiment it illustrates.
items.answer:
The figure illustrates the reaction of hydrochloric acid with washing soda (sodium carbonate). The gas evolved in the reaction is passed through lime water, which turns milky; therefore the evolved gas is carbon dioxide. Thus the experiment shows that acids decompose sodium carbonate to produce carbon dioxide:
Na₂CO₃ + 2HCl → 2NaCl + H₂O + CO₂
Ca(OH)₂ + CO₂ → CaCO₃↓ + H₂O (lime water turns milky)

items.stem: What is meant by 'water of crystallisation' of a substance? Describe an activity to show that blue copper sulphate crystals contain water of crystallisation.
items.answer:
Crystals of some compounds seem to be dry (or anhydrous), but actually contain some water molecules attached to them. This water is called water of crystallisation, and such salts are called hydrated salts.
Activity: Heat a few copper sulphate crystals in a dry boiling tube. After some time the blue colour of the crystals disappears and a white powder, anhydrous copper sulphate, is formed. A few drops of water also appear on the inner walls of the boiling tube. When some water is added to the boiling tube after heating, the blue colour reappears.
CuSO₄·5H₂O —Heat, −5H₂O→ CuSO₄ ; CuSO₄ + 5H₂O → CuSO₄·5H₂O

items.stem:
A metal is treated with dilute sulphuric acid. The gas evolved is collected by the method shown in the figure. Answer the following:
(a) Name the gas.
(b) Name the method of collection of the gas.
(c) Is the gas soluble or insoluble in water?
(d) Is the gas lighter or heavier than air?
items.answer:
(a) Hydrogen gas.
(b) The gas is collected by the downward displacement of water.
(c) Since the gas is collected over water, this suggests that the gas is insoluble in water.
(d) The gas is lighter than air, because the collecting gas jar is inverted.

items.stem: A housewife found that the cake prepared by her is hard and small in size. Which ingredient has she forgotten to add that would have made the cake fluffy? Give reason.
items.answer: She has forgotten to add baking powder during the preparation of the cake. Baking powder contains sodium hydrogen carbonate (sodium bicarbonate) and a mild edible acid such as tartaric acid. On heating, the sodium bicarbonate reacts with the acid to produce carbon dioxide gas, which gets trapped in the batter and causes the cake to rise and become soft and fluffy.

items.stem: What is meant by water of crystallisation? Explain that the crystalline salts contain water of crystallisation.
items.answer:
Water of crystallisation is the fixed number of water molecules present in one formula unit of a salt. For example, one formula unit of copper sulphate contains five water molecules (5H₂O). The water molecules which form part of the structure of a crystal are called water of crystallisation.
When hydrated salts are heated strongly, they lose their water of crystallisation. On strong heating, blue copper sulphate crystals turn white due to loss of water of crystallisation:
CuSO₄·5H₂O —Heat→ CuSO₄ + 5H₂O
(Hydrated copper sulphate, blue) (Anhydrous copper sulphate, white) (Water)
Anhydrous copper sulphate turns blue again on adding water:
CuSO₄ + 5H₂O → CuSO₄·5H₂O

items.stem: In one of the industrial processes used for manufacture of sodium hydroxide, a gas X is formed as by-product. The gas X reacts with lime water to give a compound Y which is used as a bleaching agent in chemical industry. Identify X and Y, giving the chemical equations of the reactions involved.
items.answer:
In the manufacture of sodium hydroxide (the chlor-alkali process), hydrogen gas and chlorine gas are formed as by-products; the gas X is chlorine. When chlorine gas (X) reacts with lime water it forms calcium oxychloride, i.e. bleaching powder, which is Y.
2NaCl(aq) + 2H₂O(l) → 2NaOH(aq) + Cl₂(g) + H₂(g)
X = Cl₂
Ca(OH)₂(s) + Cl₂(g) → CaOCl₂(s) + H₂O
Y = CaOCl₂, calcium oxychloride (bleaching powder)
